title: Concatenated Words
description:
# Concatenated Words

You are given an array `words` with no duplicate strings.

A concatenated word is a word that can be formed by joining at least two shorter words from the same array. The shorter words may themselves also be concatenated words, as long as they appear in `words`.

Return all concatenated words in any order. The same shorter word may be reused within a concatenation.

## Example 1:

**Input:** words = ["cat","cats","catsdogcats","dog","dogcatsdog","hippopotamuses","rat","ratcatdogcat"]

**Output:** ["catsdogcats","dogcatsdog","ratcatdogcat"]

**Explanation:** `catsdogcats` can be formed as `cats + dog + cats`; `dogcatsdog` can be formed as `dog + cats + dog`; `ratcatdogcat` can be formed as `rat + cat + dog + cat`.

## Example 2:

**Input:** words = ["cat","dog","catdog"]

**Output:** ["catdog"]

## Constraints:

* `1 <= words.length <= 10^4`
* `1 <= words[i].length <= 30`
* `words[i]` consists only of lowercase English letters.
* All strings in `words` are unique.

solutions.name: Length-Ordered Word Break DP
solutions.description:
## Approach

Sort a copy of the words by length. Before adding a word to the dictionary, run a Word Break dynamic program against only the shorter words already seen. Store every word that passes, then emit results by scanning the original input order.

## Key Insight

A concatenated word must be built from shorter words, so checking a word before inserting it prevents the word from using itself as its only piece.

## Complexity Analysis
- Time Complexity: O(n * L^3), where L is the maximum word length and substring creation costs O(L)
- Space Complexity: O(n * L)

solutions.name: HashSet DFS with Piece Count
solutions.description:
## Approach

Put every word into a hash set. For each word, run DFS over split positions. The state includes the current index and whether we have already used zero, one, or at least two pieces; memoization prevents repeated suffix work.

## Key Insight

Using the whole word as one dictionary piece is not enough. Tracking the number of pieces, capped at two, makes the at-least-two requirement explicit.

## Complexity Analysis
- Time Complexity: O(n * L^3)
- Space Complexity: O(n * L)

solutions.name: Trie-Guided Prefix DFS
solutions.description:
## Approach

Insert all words into a trie. For each candidate word, walk trie prefixes from the current index; whenever a word-ending node is found, recursively solve the suffix while counting how many pieces have been used.

## Key Insight

The trie avoids constructing every possible prefix string. It explores only prefixes that exist in the dictionary and still enforces that at least two dictionary pieces are used.

## Complexity Analysis
- Time Complexity: O(n * L^2)
- Space Complexity: O(n * L)

solutions.name: BFS over Split Positions
solutions.description:
## Approach

For each word, treat every index as a node in a graph. There is an edge from `start` to `end` when `word.substring(start, end)` is in the dictionary. Run BFS from index 0 and track whether zero, one, or at least two pieces have been used.

## Key Insight

Word Break can be viewed as reachability in a split-position graph. The answer is true only when the terminal index is reachable after at least two edges.

## Complexity Analysis
- Time Complexity: O(n * L^3)
- Space Complexity: O(n * L)

solutions.name: Minimum Piece Count DP
solutions.description:
## Approach

For each word, compute `pieces[i]`, the minimum number of dictionary words needed to build the prefix ending at index `i`. The transition skips the whole word as a single first piece. A word is concatenated when `pieces[length] >= 2`.

## Key Insight

Instead of only asking whether a prefix is reachable, this DP records the fewest pieces needed. That directly separates one-piece self matches from valid concatenations.

## Complexity Analysis
- Time Complexity: O(n * L^3)
- Space Complexity: O(n * L)
